Understanding Retention Policies in Northgate Vault

A retention policy determines how long Northgate Vault keeps a ^ before it becomes
eligible for permanent deletion. Every ^ inherits exactly one retention policy, and that
policy is resolved at the moment the ^ is created. Changing a policy later affects only
^ created after the change; it never retroactively alters the ^ date of a
^ that already exists. This behaviour is deliberate, because retroactive changes would
make it impossible to prove to an auditor what the ^ schedule was at any given point
in the past.

Policies are evaluated in a fixed order. The system first looks for a policy attached directly to
the ^. If none exists, it looks for a policy attached to the folder that contains the
^, then to that folder's parent, and so on up to the ^ root. If no policy is found
anywhere on that path, the ^ default applies. The ^ default cannot be removed,
only changed, which guarantees that every ^ always resolves to some policy.

There are three kinds of ^. Soft deletion moves the ^ to a recycle bin where it
remains visible to administrators for a further thirty days. Hard deletion removes the ^
content but keeps an immutable audit stub recording that a ^ existed, who created it, and
when it was disposed. Purge removes everything, including the audit stub, and is only available
to workspaces operating under a legal regime that requires it; most customers should never enable
purge, because it destroys the evidence that the retention policy was followed.

A legal hold suspends all ^ for the ^ it covers. Holds take precedence over
every policy, including purge, and they cannot be overridden by an administrator. Only a user with
the Legal Hold Officer role may place or release a hold, and every placement and release is
written to the audit log with the reason supplied by that user. When a hold is released, the
affected ^ return to their normal schedule; if their ^ date has already passed,
they become eligible immediately and will be processed in the next nightly sweep.

The nightly sweep runs at 02:00 in the ^'s configured timezone. It processes ^ in
creation order, oldest first, and stops after four hours regardless of how much work remains.
Anything not processed is picked up by the next sweep. Because the sweep is time-bounded rather
than work-bounded, a ^ with a very large backlog may take several nights to catch up, and
administrators sometimes mistake this for a failure. The sweep report, available under Reports and
Audit, shows exactly how many ^ were considered, how many were disposed, and how many
remained in the queue when the sweep stopped.

Two questions come up repeatedly in support tickets. The first is why a ^ with an expired
^ date is still visible. Almost always the answer is either an active legal hold or a
backlogged sweep, both of which the sweep report will show. The second is whether a retention
policy can be shortened. It can, but only for future ^, and the interface deliberately
makes this awkward in order to prevent an administrator from accidentally believing that existing
^ have been reshuffled onto the shorter schedule.
